title: Building Your Own Product: Idea to Launch
subtitle: Four outcomes: submit an idea, talk to customers, ship a product, name the brand.
description: The only builder studio in the library. You leave with four artifacts on this device: a locked idea, interview notes from a real person, a live product URL, and a brand plus first-user list. Other courses stay on Git and pitching — this one is the build.
outcomes: Idea submitted — one problem, one customer, locked for the month
Customers talked to — notes from a real conversation, not a survey
Product built — a live URL someone else can click
Brand named — a promise people can repeat, plus the first 20 users

modules.title: Week 1: Submit the idea
modules.summary: Lock one problem and one customer. Everything later in this course is about this idea.

lessons.title: How to Get and Evaluate Startup Ideas | Startup School
lessons.description: Jared Friedman’s questions you apply to a real idea this week: who already needs this, why you, why now. Pause after each question and write the answer you will submit.

lessons.title: Lean Canvas Template
lessons.description: Fill problem, customer, UVP, and channel before you write code. Empty boxes mean the idea is not submitted yet.

lessons.title: Outcome 1: Submit your idea
lessons.description: Hand in the idea you will build for the rest of this course. After this, changing the customer is a rewrite, not a tweak.

assignment.brief: Pick one problem a named person already has. This submission is the brief for weeks 2–4 — interviews, the product URL, and the brand all have to match it.
assignment.deliverable: A locked idea a classmate could explain back to you.

fields.label: The idea in one sentence
fields.hint: Name the job, not the category. ‘It’s an AI platform’ is not an idea.

fields.label: The first customer (a real type of person, not ‘everyone’)
fields.placeholder: Second-year students who already… / shop owners on Instagram who…
fields.hint: If you cannot picture where they sit on a Tuesday, it is too wide.

fields.label: Why this is a real problem (something they already do or pay for)
fields.placeholder: They currently use WhatsApp + a notebook, and last week they…
fields.hint: Past behavior. ‘They would love this’ does not count.

fields.label: What you will not build this month
fields.placeholder: No mobile app / no payments / no admin / no second customer type…
fields.hint: If this list is empty, you have not submitted an idea — you have submitted a wishlist.

checklist: A stranger can say the one-liner back.
The customer is narrow enough to find this week.
You named something they already do, not a compliment they might give.
You cut work you will refuse.

lessons.title: Week 1 Assessment: Idea worth submitting
lessons.description: What makes an idea worth locking for a month.

questions.prompt: The strongest signal an idea is worth submitting is:

options.text: It sounds impressive when you pitch it at a party.
You (or people you can name) already feel this problem and already work around it.
No one has ever tried anything like it.
It requires the least possible work to build.

questions.explanation: Submit problems people already live with. Novelty and ease are not the test.

questions.prompt: A submitted idea should usually name:

options.text: Every feature on the year-one roadmap.
One customer, one job, and what you will not build yet.
A company name and a logo only.
A fundraising target.

questions.explanation: The submission is a constraint: who, what job, and the cuts.

questions.prompt: Select every section that belongs on a Lean Canvas before you build.

options.text: Problem
Unique Value Proposition
Office lease terms
Customer segment

questions.explanation: Problem, customer, UVP, channel, and metrics — not operations.

modules.title: Week 2: Talk to a customer
modules.summary: Run a Mom Test conversation about the idea you submitted. Notes beat opinions.

lessons.title: The Mom Test: how to talk to customers without lying to yourself
lessons.description: Rob Fitzpatrick on the three rules: talk about their life, ask about the last time (not ‘would you’), and listen more than you pitch. Pause and write the questions you will actually ask.

lessons.title: How To Talk To Users | Startup School
lessons.description: How to find people, book the call, and turn notes into a build/kill decision — without pitching first.

lessons.title: Outcome 2: Talk to a customer
lessons.description: Interview one real person about the idea you submitted. Write what they already do — not whether they like your pitch.

assignment.brief: Use the idea from week 1. Talk about their last week, not your solution. Best prompt: ‘Walk me through the last time this happened.’ A scheduled interview with a full script counts if you name the person and the time.
assignment.deliverable: Proof you talked to a customer: eight questions, notes, and a keep / kill / rewrite.

fields.label: Who you are interviewing and the last time they hit this problem
fields.placeholder: Name / role — last Tuesday they … and they used …
fields.hint: A real person. ‘Students in general’ is not an interview.

fields.label: Eight Mom Test questions you will ask
fields.placeholder:
1. Walk me through the last time…
2. What did you try?
3. What did that cost you?
…
fields.hint: Ban ‘Would you use this?’ and ‘Is this a good idea?’

fields.label: Interview notes (or the scheduled script if the call is this week)
fields.placeholder: They currently… They already paid for… They refused to… Commitment they offered…
fields.hint: Write behavior and commitments. Compliments do not count as signal.

fields.label: Keep / kill / rewrite the submitted idea — what changed
fields.placeholder: Decision: keep / kill / rewrite because they already… The one-liner is now …
fields.hint: If nothing about the idea moved, you pitched instead of interviewing.

checklist: You named a person, not a demographic.
None of the eight questions pitch the product.
Notes include something they already do or already pay for.
The keep / kill / rewrite names what you heard.

lessons.title: Week 2 Assessment: Talking to customers
lessons.description: Mom Test rules and what belongs on a Lean Canvas.

questions.prompt: Which question is most likely to pass the Mom Test?

options.text: Would you use an app that does this?
Walk me through the last time this problem showed up. What did you do?
Isn’t this a great idea?
On a scale of 1–10, how excited are you?

questions.explanation: Ask about a specific past episode and what they already did. Opinions and compliments are polite lies.

questions.prompt: What is the primary goal of an early user interview?

options.text: Convince the user your idea is good.
Understand their current behavior and pain points without pitching your solution.
Get them to pre-pay immediately.
Ask only yes/no questions to save time.

questions.explanation: Good interviews focus on understanding existing behavior and pain. Pitching too early biases the feedback you get.

questions.prompt: Select every habit that belongs in a customer conversation.

options.text: Ask about the last time the problem showed up.
Write down what they already do or already pay for.
Pitch the full product in the first two minutes.
End by asking for a small commitment (intro, follow-up, a try).

questions.explanation: Past behavior and a real next step beat a pitch. Compliments are not signal.

modules.title: Week 3: Build the product
modules.summary: Ship the smallest version of the submitted idea. The outcome is a URL, not a spec.

lessons.title: Michael Seibel — How to Plan an MVP
lessons.description: What actually counts as an MVP: the smallest thing that delivers value to a few users. Pause and delete features from your list as he talks.

lessons.title: Value Proposition Canvas (fill this, 5 min)
lessons.description: Alex Osterwalder’s official walkthrough: customer jobs, pains, gains vs your pain relievers and gain creators. If a box is empty, that feature is not in the MVP.

lessons.title: Outcome 3: Build the product (live URL)
lessons.description: Ship something a stranger can click: a site, form, bot, or demo. A spec without a URL does not count.

assignment.brief: Build the idea from week 1 using whatever is fastest — Carrd, Notion, Google Form, WhatsApp flow, Replit, Next.js. Ugly is fine. Private-only Figma is not a product.
assignment.deliverable: A live URL plus what it does and who already clicked it.

fields.label: Live product URL
fields.placeholder: https://… (or a public form / bot / demo link)
fields.hint: Must open without a login you cannot share. If it is a WhatsApp number or form, write the exact link or handle.

fields.label: What a user can do in 60 seconds
fields.placeholder: They land → they … → they get … That is the only job.
fields.hint: One job from the submitted idea. If you need a tutorial, it is too big.

fields.label: How you built it (tools + what you cut)
fields.placeholder: Built in … I skipped accounts / payments / mobile because…
fields.hint: Name the stack. Name the cuts. ‘I used AI’ is not a build log.

fields.label: Who already used it (name + what they did)
fields.placeholder: I sent it to [name]. They … They got stuck on … Next I will …
fields.hint: At least one real person. ‘I will share later’ fails the outcome.

checklist: The URL opens for someone who is not you.
The job matches the idea you submitted.
You named what you refused to build.
A named person already tried it.

lessons.title: Week 3 Assessment: Shipping an MVP
lessons.description: Scoping an MVP and problem–solution fit.

questions.prompt: Per Michael Seibel's MVP framework, what should your first MVP optimize for?

options.text: Supporting every feature you can imagine.
The smallest thing you can ship to test if you can deliver real value to a few users.
A polished, investor-ready product.
Building for a huge, general audience from day one.

questions.explanation: Seibel's advice: launch something ridiculously simple to a narrow set of early users first, then iterate on what you learn.

questions.prompt: On the Value Proposition Canvas, problem–solution fit means:

options.text: You listed as many features as the competitor.
Your pain relievers and gain creators match jobs, pains, and gains you observed.
You registered a domain.
Investors liked the deck.

questions.explanation: Fit is when the value map hits real jobs, pains, and gains — not when the feature list is long.

questions.prompt: Select every habit that matches 'launch something bad quickly' thinking.

options.text: Ship a limited version to a small set of users this week.
Delay launch until every edge case is handled.
Treat the first release as a way to learn, not a finished product.
Talk to the first users again after they try it.

questions.explanation: MVP thinking favors fast, narrow releases you learn from, not indefinite polishing before anyone sees it.

modules.title: Week 4: Build the brand and get first users
modules.summary: Name the promise, write the launch post, and put the live product in front of 20 people.

lessons.title: How to Get Your First Customers | Startup School
lessons.description: Gustaf Alströmer’s founder sales loop: make a list, send a short note, run a demo, track drop-off. Pause and start the spreadsheet of 20 names.

lessons.title: How to Launch on Product Hunt (Official Guide)
lessons.description: Product Hunt’s own walkthrough of preparing a hunter, a first comment, and a live URL — do this after friends already use the product.

lessons.title: Outcome 4: Brand + first 20 users
lessons.description: Write the brand promise for the product you shipped, then put that URL in front of 20 people.

assignment.brief: Brand is the sentence people repeat when you are not in the room. Pair it with the live URL from week 3 and a list of people you will actually message.
assignment.deliverable: A brand promise, a launch post with the product URL, and a named first-20 list.

fields.label: Brand promise (one sentence people can repeat)
fields.placeholder: For [who], we are the [category] that [unique outcome].
fields.hint: If it still works after you swap in a rival’s name, it is not a brand yet.

fields.label: The first 20 people or rooms who will see the live product
fields.placeholder:
Day 1–3: message these people…
Day 4–7: post in this room…
Link I will send: …
fields.hint: Names, groups, or shops. Include the product URL. ‘Go viral’ is not a plan.

fields.label: The short note you will send (paste-ready)
fields.placeholder: Hey [name] — I built X because you said Y. Can you try this URL this week and tell me if Z still hurts?
fields.hint: About their last problem, the live URL, one ask.

fields.label: Launch post — tagline, who it’s for, product URL
fields.placeholder:
Tagline: …
Who it’s for: …
Link: …
Maker comment: …
fields.hint: A stranger should know what to click. The link must be the thing you built.

checklist: The promise is specific enough to reject customers.
The 20-user plan names people or rooms and includes the live URL.
The note asks for a try, not a compliment.
The launch post has a tagline and the product link.

lessons.title: Week 4 Assessment: Brand & first users
lessons.description: Founder-led sales and launching as a repeatable process.

questions.prompt: For your first customers, Gustaf’s Startup School advice is to:

options.text: Buy ads before you can describe the buyer.
Make a list of the easiest likely buyers, message them yourself, and track each step of the funnel.
Wait until the product is famous.
Hire a salesperson in week one.

questions.explanation: First customers are founder-led and unscalable: a list, a note, a demo, and numbers on drop-off.

questions.prompt: Per Product Hunt's official launch guide, which practice most improves a launch?

options.text: Submitting with no prior engagement on the platform.
Participating in the community and building relationships before launch day.
Launching without a live product URL.
Avoiding all outside promotion.

questions.explanation: Product Hunt recommends genuine, sustained participation (comments, upvotes, feedback) well before your own launch, not a cold submission.

questions.prompt: Select every legitimate way to 'launch again' for an existing product.

options.text: Announcing a major new feature.
Re-launching to a new audience or platform.
Reposting the exact same launch post daily.
Sharing a milestone (users, revenue, an integration) as its own moment.

questions.explanation: Each real update, audience, or milestone is a legitimate reason to launch again — spamming the same post isn't.
